Peter speaks to his own generation; Jesus said Elijah 'restores all things' (Matthew 17:11) and connected the end with that generation.
Critics note the language of creation-wide restoration (Romans 8:21) has no clear fulfilment in AD 70, and the view's denial of a future return is outside the historic creeds.
Scoffers, Delay and New Heavens and Earth

Peter warns that scoffers will come in the last days asking where the promise of Christ's coming is. He answers that as the world was once destroyed by water, so the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire; that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years; that the delay is patience; and that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, when the heavens pass away with a roar, the elements (stoicheia) dissolve with heat and the earth and its works 'will be found' (or 'burned up', a textual variant). Believers wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells.

Is this the final conflagration and renewal of the physical cosmos at the Second Coming, or covenantal language for the end of the old covenant order in AD 70? And does the fire annihilate creation or purge and renew it?

The final Day of the Lord at Christ's return, when the present cosmos is judged and purified by fire and renewed as the new heavens and new earth; the delay is God's patience during the whole age. Most Reformed amillennialists read 3:10 'will be found' (heurethēsetai) as laying bare for judgment, and the fire as purifying rather than annihilating.

The parallel with the Flood (3:5–7), which judged but did not annihilate the world, points to cosmic renewal; Romans 8:21 and Revelation 21:1 confirm the hope; 'a thousand years as a day' assumes a long delay is possible.

Partial and full preterists argue that 'heavens and earth' can be covenantal-political language (Isaiah 51:15–16), and that stoicheia elsewhere means the elementary principles of the old order (Galatians 4:3, 9; Colossians 2:8, 20).

Many postmillennialists, including Gentry and Mathison, read 3:10–13 as the final consummation at Christ's single bodily return, after the long era of gospel advance; the 'delay' allows the gospel to prosper for a long age. Peter's appeal to creation and the Flood points to the material cosmos, not merely the Jewish order.

Peter grounds his argument in the physical creation and the global Flood (3:5–6), and the new heavens and earth are a place 'where righteousness dwells', a consummate state (Isaiah 65:17 language here applied to its final form).

Other postmillennial preterists counter that the 'last days' and scoffers fit the generation before AD 70 (Matthew 24:48); Gentry answers that Peter's anticipating a long time span ('a thousand years as a day') points beyond that generation.

Some partial preterists (e.g. Leithart) read the passing 'heavens and earth' as the old covenant world, with its temple and elemental ordinances, dissolved in AD 70; the new heavens and new earth are the new covenant order. John Owen, in a sermon on 3:11, had already applied the dissolving heavens and earth to the Jewish church-state.

Isaiah uses 'heavens and earth' for the covenant order (Isaiah 51:16; 65:17 is followed by a world still containing death, 65:20); 'the last days' (3:3) refers to the end of the old covenant age (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26); stoicheia means elementary religious principles elsewhere in Paul.

Other partial preterists, such as Gentry, reject this reading because Peter compares the coming judgment with the Flood and creation itself. Critics also note that the passage appears in a letter that expects a long delay, the opposite of the near-coming emphasis in Matthew 24.

The passage describes the passing of the old covenant world in AD 70; the new heavens and new earth of 3:13 are the new covenant realm in which righteousness dwells now, and there is no future cosmic conflagration.

Don Preston argues that Peter's 'promise' comes from the prophets (3:2), whose new creation oracles (Isaiah 65–66) concerned Israel's covenant world, and that Jesus limited 'heaven and earth passing' to his generation (Matthew 24:34–35).

Critics, including partial preterists, argue that Peter's cosmic Flood analogy, the global judgment of 'the ungodly' and the scope of the new creation exceed AD 70; the view's denial of a future Second Coming and judgment places it outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

The Day of the Lord is an extended period beginning with the Tribulation and running through the millennium; the dissolution of the heavens and earth by fire comes at its end, after the millennium and the final judgment, preparing for the eternal state of Revelation 21.
'A day is as a thousand years' (3:8) is sometimes linked to the thousand-year span of the Day of the Lord; Revelation 20:11–21:1 places the passing of heaven and earth after the millennium.
Critics say that stretching 'the day' across a thousand years blurs Peter's point that the day comes suddenly, 'like a thief' (3:10).

The final conflagration and renewal follow the millennial reign of Christ and the last judgment; Peter does not mention the millennium because his concern is the certainty of the final day against scoffers.
Fits the sequence of Revelation 20–21 while reading 2 Peter 3 as the final state.
Amillennialists argue that 2 Peter 3 links Christ's coming directly to the cosmic renewal, leaving no space for an intervening millennium.
Old Covenant Ready to Vanish Away

After quoting Jeremiah 31:31–34 at length, the author says that by speaking of a 'new' covenant God has made the first obsolete, and what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near (engys) to disappearing.

If the old covenant was made obsolete at the cross, why is it still 'near to disappearing' when Hebrews is written? Does this point to the temple's destruction in AD 70 as the visible end of the old covenant order, and what follows for eschatology?

The old covenant was made obsolete in principle by Christ's death, but its institutions, the temple and sacrifices, were still standing and about to vanish; that happened in AD 70. Hebrews thus stands in a forty-year 'transition generation' between the old and new covenant eras, and it supports reading the 'last days' as the end of the old covenant age (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26).

The present tense of the participles ('becoming obsolete and growing old') and engys ('near') imply an imminent historical event; the letter assumes the sacrifices still continue (10:1–3), and many date it before 70.

Some amillennialists respond that the verse may describe the inherent temporariness of the old order rather than predict AD 70. Preterists answer that the author's 'yet a little while' (10:37) and 'the Day drawing near' (10:25) supply the timeframe.

The covenant transition, begun at the cross, was completed only in AD 70, when the old covenant world passed; that moment was the arrival of the 'age to come', the resurrection and the Parousia (9:28). Since the old covenant vanished then, all eschatological promises tied to it were fulfilled then as well.
The 'nearness' of 8:13 combined with 'he who is coming will come and will not delay' (10:37) and Christ appearing a 'second time' (9:28) are read as one event.

Critics accept that 8:13 points to AD 70 but deny that the end of the temple equals the bodily resurrection and final judgment; they note that Hebrews 9:27–28 links the second appearing to the judgment after death. The denial of a future return places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

The old covenant became obsolete with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, and the passing of its shadows was sealed by the destruction of the temple. This does not end the age: the church lives in the 'last days' between Christ's first and second comings and awaits the city to come (13:14).
Hebrews 9:9–10 calls the old system a symbol 'until the time of reformation'; Lane and others date Hebrews in the 60s and see 8:13 as alert to the temple's coming end.

Partial preterists press that the amillennial view underplays how much New Testament 'nearness' language is tied to AD 70; amillennialists answer that a near judgment does not exhaust the hope of the age to come.

The Mosaic covenant as a rule of life ended at the cross; the new covenant, made with Israel and Judah, is now applied spiritually to the church, but it will be fulfilled nationally with Israel at Christ's return. The obsolescence of the old covenant does not imply that God's promises to national Israel are cancelled.
Jeremiah 31's new covenant is addressed to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah'; progressive dispensationalists hold one new covenant with present (church) and future (Israel) phases.

Critics ask how this squares with a millennial temple and sacrifices (Ezekiel 40–48) after the old covenant has 'vanished'. Dispensationalists answer that millennial worship belongs to the new covenant, not a revival of the Mosaic covenant.

The decisive end of the old covenant in AD 70 vindicated Christ and cleared the stage for the new covenant kingdom to advance among the nations; the 'better covenant' (8:6) with its law written on hearts is the engine of the gospel's progressive success.
Jeremiah 31:34 promises that 'all shall know me, from the least to the greatest', which postmillennialists take as an expanding reality as the new covenant spreads.
Amillennialists read 'all shall know me' as describing every member of the new covenant community, not an eventual majority of humankind.
Mount Zion and the Unshakable Kingdom

Believers 'have come' not to Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to innumerable angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. God promises, quoting Haggai 2:6, 'yet once more' to shake not only the earth but heaven, removing what is shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain; since we are receiving (present participle) an unshakable kingdom, we should worship with reverence.
Is the 'shaking' of heaven and earth the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, the final cosmic judgment, or both? And how does the present 'have come to Zion' relate to future hope?

The 'shaking' that removes what is made is the dismantling of the old covenant order, climaxing in AD 70, while the church is already receiving the unshakable kingdom. Haggai 2:6–7 was originally about the shaking of nations and the glory of the latter temple, which the author sees fulfilled in the new covenant.
'Receiving' is present tense; 8:13 says the old order is near to disappearing; the contrast throughout chapter 12 is between Sinai and Zion, two covenants, not two cosmic eras.

Critics note that 12:26 says God will shake 'heaven' as well as earth, and that 12:27 speaks of removing 'created things', which suggests the final cosmic judgment. Partial preterists answer that the language is covenantal, as in the prophets.

An inaugurated eschatology: believers have already come to heavenly Zion, joined to the assembly in heaven, while the final shaking of heaven and earth at Christ's return will remove the present created order in its fallen form and leave the unshakable kingdom fully revealed. AD 70 may be a foreshadowing, but the 'yet once more' points to the consummation.

'Yet once more' (12:27) signals a final, once-for-all event; Hebrews elsewhere locates the believer's hope in a city 'to come' (13:14) and a 'second appearing' (9:28); Vos saw Hebrews as the classic expression of the 'already' heavenly participation.
Preterists argue that 'shaking' language in Haggai referred to historical upheaval among nations; amillennialists respond that Hebrews deliberately widens it to heaven and earth.

The present reception of the unshakable kingdom guarantees its triumph: what is shaken (the old order and every opposing power) is removed, while Christ's kingdom remains and advances until all is subject to him; the passage grounds confidence, not retreat.

The removal of the old and the permanence of the new fit Daniel 2:44 (a kingdom that will never be destroyed) and Christ's present reign (Hebrews 1:13; 10:12–13, 'waiting until his enemies are made a footstool').
Amillennialists agree that the kingdom is unshakable but deny that this entails visible historical dominance before the end.

The heavenly Jerusalem is the present spiritual position of the church and the future dwelling of the saints (Revelation 21:2), distinct from the earthly Jerusalem of the millennium; the final shaking occurs at the end of the age, through the Tribulation judgments and the passing of heaven and earth. The passage does not replace Israel's earthly Zion promises.
Hebrews speaks of a heavenly city, which dispensationalists distinguish from the earthly city promised to Israel (Zechariah 14; Isaiah 2).
Covenant theologians reply that the author contrasts the earthly Sinai with the heavenly Zion precisely to wean readers from earthly Jerusalem (13:12–14).
The shaking was entirely completed in AD 70; the unshakable kingdom fully came then, and believers now dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem with no further cosmic shaking to come.

'Yet a little while' (10:37) and the near disappearance of the old (8:13) fix the timeframe. Proponents add that the 'things that have been made' which are removed (12:27) echo Hebrews' language for the handmade earthly sanctuary (9:11, 24), pointing to the temple order rather than the physical cosmos.

Critics object that the passage contrasts the created order with what is unshakable, a cosmic distinction that AD 70 did not effect; the denial of a future consummation places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.
Perilous Times in the Last Days

Paul tells Timothy that in the last days difficult (chalepoi) times will come: people will be lovers of self and money, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, lovers of pleasure rather than God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. 'Avoid such people', he adds (3:5); such teachers will 'not get very far', for their folly will be plain (3:9).

Is this a forecast of moral decline at the end of the church age, a description of the whole interadvent era, or a picture of the apostolic generation before AD 70? What does it imply for optimism or pessimism about history?

A prophecy of the moral and spiritual decline that will characterize the end of the church age, especially in professing Christendom, as part of the apostasy before the Lord's return (2 Thessalonians 2:3; 1 Timothy 4:1). Many see present cultural trends as a sign that the end is near.
Paul's future tenses ('will come', 'will be'); parallels in Matthew 24:12 and Luke 18:8; the description of religious form without power fits an apostate church.

Critics note that Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people (3:5) and describes them as already present in Ephesus (3:6–8), which shows the 'last days' include Timothy's day. Dispensationalists reply that present instances foreshadow an intensified final form.

The 'last days' span the whole period from Christ's first coming to his return (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18); the vices Paul lists recur throughout church history and may intensify near the end, but they mark the age as a whole rather than one final phase. Believers face them with Scripture (3:14–17), not alarm.
Paul applies the warning to Timothy's present ministry (3:5–9); Towner and others read the 'last days' as already under way in Ephesus.
Dispensationalists argue that the future tense points beyond Timothy's day; postmillennialists ask whether the amillennial reading leaves room for real cultural progress.

The 'last days' are the whole new covenant era, and Paul describes 'seasons' (kairoi) of difficulty within it, not unrelieved decline. Crucially, 3:9 says such people 'will not get very far' because their folly will be exposed: error is real but self-limiting, while the gospel advances.
The plural kairoi suggests recurring periods; 3:9 limits the progress of evil; the context sends Timothy to preach the word, which equips for every good work (3:16–4:2).

Amillennialists and premillennialists see 3:13 ('evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse') as signalling persistent or growing evil; postmillennialists answer that 3:13 describes the impostors' own trajectory, not society's overall direction.

The 'last days' are the final days of the old covenant age, the forty years from the cross to AD 70; Paul warns Timothy about conditions in the church and society of his own generation, which climaxed in the apostasy and judgment Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:10–12).
Paul instructs Timothy personally to avoid these people; the description matches the turmoil of the 60s; Hebrews 1:2 and 1 Peter 1:20 place the 'last times' in the apostolic era.
Amillennialists accept the present application but argue the last days continue until Christ's return (1 Corinthians 10:11; Hebrews 9:26 speaks of the 'end of the ages' as begun, not ended).

The last days began with Christ, and the vices of 3:1–5 will mark the whole age, culminating in a final apostasy and the Antichrist before Christ returns to establish his kingdom; the passage calls for vigilance throughout.
Combines the present application (3:5–9) with the future intensification pointed to in 2 Thessalonians 2.
Postmillennialists object that this assumes a final decline the text does not require.
Things That Must Soon Take Place

Revelation opens and closes with time markers: it reveals 'the things that must soon (en tachei) take place' (1:1; 22:6), 'the time is near' (engys, 1:3; 22:10), and John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy (22:10), in contrast to Daniel, who was told to seal his vision because it concerned a distant time (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9). Jesus says 'I am coming soon' (22:7, 12, 20).
How should 'soon' and 'near' govern the interpretation of the book? They are the central texts for preterism, and every school must give an account of them.

The time markers are meant literally and frame the book: most of Revelation's prophecies (especially chs. 4–19) were fulfilled soon after writing, in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 and the Roman crisis around it. On the early date (c. 65–66) that most partial preterists hold, 'soon' meant within a few years. Chapters 20–22 extend to the present age and the final consummation.

The markers stand at both ends of the book as bookends; the contrast with Daniel's sealing (Daniel 12:4) shows the time had arrived; the first readers were seven real churches promised blessing for heeding what was near (1:3).

Critics ask why the time texts should be strict for chapters 4–19 but not for 20–22, which also lie within the bracketing statements. Partial preterists answer that the book itself signals long-term developments (a 'thousand years', 20:2–7). The date of Revelation is also disputed (pre-70 vs c. 95).

Because the same time markers bracket the whole book, everything in it, including the Second Coming, resurrection, judgment and new creation of chs. 19–22, was fulfilled by AD 70. Consistency forbids splitting the book, as partial preterists do.
Jesus says 'I am coming soon' in chapter 22 itself (22:7, 12, 20), right alongside the new Jerusalem visions; J. Stuart Russell's The Parousia pressed this consistency argument.

Critics reply that 'coming soon' language can describe impending comings in judgment within history (as in 2:5, 16) without being the final coming, and that the denial of a future bodily return and resurrection places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

'En tachei' can mean 'quickly' or 'suddenly', describing the rapidity of the events when they begin, not their nearness; and 'near' is measured from God's perspective, for whom a thousand years is as a day (2 Peter 3:8). The events of chs. 4–22 lie mostly in the future, and the church is to live in imminent expectation.

The same phrase en tachei is used of rapid action in Luke 18:8 and Acts 12:7; the New Testament treats the Lord's return as imminent yet not dated; the book's scope (global judgments, Satan's binding, new creation) exceeds any first-century event.

Preterists reply that 'near' (engys) is not a word about manner, and that a two-thousand-year delay strips the time markers of meaning for the first readers. Futurists answer that imminence is real: the next event on God's calendar could come at any time.

The prophecies began to be fulfilled soon after John wrote and then unfold in sequence through church history, from imperial Rome through the fall of the empire, the rise of the papacy and Islam, to the end; 'soon' refers to the beginning of the chain, which started in John's day.
Accounts for the time markers without collapsing the book into one generation, and gives the book relevance to every era of history as a continuous prophecy.

Critics note that historicist schemes have disagreed widely and repeatedly had to be revised as predicted end dates passed, and that the first readers could hardly identify fulfilments centuries later.

'Soon' expresses the inaugurated nature of the last days: with Christ's death and resurrection, the latter days of Daniel have begun (Revelation 1:1 echoes Daniel 2:28–29, replacing 'in the latter days' with 'soon'). The book's symbols describe the conflict of Christ and Satan throughout the whole age, every part of which is 'near' to the end.

Beale notes that Revelation 1:1 alludes to Daniel 2 and changes 'latter days' to 'soon', implying that Daniel's kingdom prophecy has begun to be fulfilled; Hendriksen's 'progressive parallelism' reads each cycle as covering the whole age.
Preterists say this dissolves concrete time markers into a general nearness; futurists say it loses the book's prophetic specificity.

The book addressed real first-century crises and promised that the decisive events had begun, but its climax, Christ's coming, the millennium and the new creation, remains future; prophetic perspective telescopes near and far events, as the Old Testament prophets did.
Ladd combined preterist and futurist elements: the beast of chapter 13 is both Rome and the end-time Antichrist.
Preterists see the telescoping theory as an escape; idealists see it as unnecessarily concrete.
The Beasts of Revelation 13 and the Number 666

A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea; the dragon gives it his power and throne. One head seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole earth marvels. It blasphemes and makes war on the saints for forty-two months. A second beast, from the land, with lamb-like horns but a dragon's voice (later called the false prophet, 19:20), performs signs, causes an image of the first beast to be worshipped, and requires a mark on the right hand or forehead for buying and selling. The beast's number is 'the number of a man': 666 (13:18), though some ancient witnesses read 616.
Who or what is the beast: Nero and the Roman Empire, the papacy, a future Antichrist, or the persecuting state in every age? How does the number 666, and the variant 616, fit each view?

The sea beast is the Roman Empire and, as one of its heads, Nero Caesar, the first emperor to persecute Christians (AD 64–68), whose campaign lasted about forty-two months (late 64 to June 68). The number confirms it: spelled in Hebrew letters as nrwn qsr (Nero Caesar), the name totals 666 (50+200+6+50+100+60+200); in the Latin form Nero, without the final n (50), it totals 616, which explains the ancient variant. The land beast is a local power promoting emperor worship, variously the provincial imperial cult in Asia or (Chilton) Jerusalem's leadership collaborating with Rome.

The spelling nrwn qsr is attested in an Aramaic document from Wadi Murabba'at (Hillers), and the 616 variant, known to Irenaeus and found in P115 (the oldest papyrus of Revelation 13) and Codex Ephraemi, is best explained by a scribe adjusting for the Latin spelling. Revelation calls the number one 'for one who has understanding' (13:18), a puzzle the first readers could solve. Bauckham, not a preterist, also accepts the Nero gematria.

Critics note that Irenaeus, who knew the 616 variant, never suggested Nero; that a Greek-speaking audience is asked to compute in Hebrew letters; and that the Hebrew form 'qsr' is a defective spelling. Proponents answer that John's Greek is full of Hebrew idiom (e.g. Abaddon, 9:11; Armageddon, 16:16), and that the Murabba'at text shows the spelling was in use.

The sea beast is the persecuting political power of every age, with Rome as John's present example; the land beast is false religion and propaganda that serves it. 666 is symbolic: six falls short of seven (completeness), so triple six signifies the beast's persistent failure to be divine despite its imitation of the Trinity. Many idealists allow that John may have used a Nero gematria as a pointer to the type.

The dragon, sea beast and land beast form a parody of Father, Son and Spirit; the beast's 'death wound' parodies the slain Lamb (5:6; 13:3); John's numbers elsewhere are symbolic (7, 12, 144,000). Bauckham notes 666 is a triangular number (the sum of 1 to 36) and that 'beast' (thērion) spelled in Hebrew also totals 666.

Preterists argue that 'the number of a man' (13:18) calls for an individual identification; futurists say the symbolic reading empties the specific details (a mark, an image, a forty-two-month reign).

The sea beast is a future world ruler, the Antichrist, who heads a revived form of the Roman Empire (ten horns, Daniel 7:7–8, 24) and persecutes believers for the last three and a half years of Daniel's seventieth week. The healed head may be a literal recovery from apparent death or a revived empire; the land beast is a future religious leader; the mark is a literal means of economic control. The number will identify the man when he appears; past calculations have been premature.

The beast's universal worship (13:8), its specific forty-two-month span matching Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, and its destruction at Christ's return (19:19–20) point to events not yet fulfilled; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–8 describes a future 'man of lawlessness'.

Preterists and idealists reply that John's first readers were told to calculate the number (13:18), which would be meaningless if it concerned someone two thousand years later; futurists answer that the instruction is addressed to all who read the prophecy, including the last generation.

The sea beast is the papacy as a politico-religious power that arose from the fallen Roman Empire; the forty-two months are 1,260 years on the day-for-a-year principle (often dated 538–1798, from Justinian's era to the French capture of Pope Pius VI). The land beast is the papal hierarchy or, in some versions, a later power. 666 has been read as Lateinos (Greek for 'the Latin [man/kingdom]', 30+1+300+5+10+50+70+200 = 666), a suggestion first made by Irenaeus and favoured by Elliott; Adventist writers popularized the title 'Vicarius Filii Dei'.

Luther, Calvin and many later Protestant commentators identified the papacy with the Antichrist powers of Daniel 7 and Revelation 13; Daniel 7's little horn rising after the fourth empire fits a power arising from Rome; the computation in Lateinos goes back to Irenaeus.

Critics note that 'Vicarius Filii Dei' is not an official papal title, that many different names can be made to total 666, and that the 1,260-year dates shift between historicist writers. Historicists answer that the convergence of the chronology with the history of papal temporal power is striking.

The beast is both Rome in John's day and the eschatological Antichrist in whom the persecuting power will culminate before Christ's return; Ladd saw Nero redivivus legends in the background and held that the fulfilment is still future. The number may allude to Nero as a type of the final Antichrist.
Reflects how biblical prophecy often has a near historical referent and a future culmination (compare Antiochus Epiphanes in Daniel 11).
Preterists consider the future extension unnecessary; futurists consider the Roman reference too strong a concession.

Postmillennialists mostly follow the preterist identification of the beast with Nero and Rome: the beast was defeated in the first century, Christ's kingdom triumphed over imperial Rome, and the church need not fear a future world dictator. Others, such as James Jordan and Peter Leithart, propose alternative backgrounds for 666, notably the 666 talents of gold Solomon received yearly (1 Kings 10:14), which marks a king corrupted by wealth and power.
The Solomonic reading fits the economic stress of 13:16–17 and the Old Testament background John uses everywhere; it is offered alongside or instead of the Nero calculation.

Critics of the Solomon reading note that 1 Kings 10:14 involves talents, not a man's name, whereas 13:18 calls it the number of a man and a name (13:17). Futurists add that a first-century fulfilment cannot account for the beast's final destruction at Christ's return (19:19–20).
The Harlot, the Seven Hills and the Seven Kings

An angel shows John a woman, 'Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes', drunk with the blood of the saints, sitting on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. The angel explains that the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits and also seven kings: 'five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain a little while'; the beast that was and is not is an eighth, yet 'of the seven' (17:9–11). The ten horns are kings who later hate the harlot and burn her (17:16), and the woman is 'the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (17:18).

Who is the harlot (Rome, Jerusalem, papal Rome, or a future system)? Do the seven kings let us date Revelation by identifying the king who 'is'? The date of Revelation is disputed: early (c. 65–68, before Jerusalem's fall) or late (c. 95, under Domitian, following Irenaeus).

The seven kings are Roman emperors counted from Julius Caesar, as Josephus, Suetonius and others counted: Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius and Claudius have fallen; Nero (54–68) 'is'; Galba, who reigned only about seven months (68–69), is the one who 'remains a little while'. Revelation was therefore written under Nero, before AD 70. Many (Chilton, Gentry, Leithart) identify the harlot as apostate Jerusalem, allied with and riding on the Roman beast, which finally turned and destroyed her in AD 70 (17:16).
